o: It forms within the substance of psoas major
Most branches emerge laterally. The genitofemoral emerges anteriorly, and the obturator and lumbosacral trunk medially.
The femoral nerve is formed from the posterior divisions of L2, L3 and L4
The obturator nerve is from the anterior divisions.
The accessory obturator nerve, when present, supplies pectineus
Last's: from the posterior divisions of L3 and L4, present in about a third. It would better be called an accessory femoral nerve.
The genitofemoral nerve emerges from the lateral border of psoas
It emerges from the anterior surface of psoas and runs down on it, deep to the psoas fascia.
Its genital branch supplies cremaster
It enters the coverings of the spermatic cord through the deep ring region.
Its femoral branch supplies skin below the middle of the inguinal ligament
It enters the femoral sheath in front of the femoral artery.
It is crossed by the ureter and gonadal vessels
On the left also by the left colic vessels and inferior mesenteric vein.
It is motor to sartorius
The femoral branch has no motor fibres. Sartorius is supplied by the femoral nerve.
Arises from the posterior divisions of L2 and L3 or from the femoral nerve
Last's gives both possible origins.
Enters the thigh about 1 cm medial to the anterior superior iliac spine
In a tunnel behind or through the inguinal ligament.
May be compressed to cause meralgia paraesthetica
Also traction from transversus fibres arising from the iliac fascia.
Supplies the skin of the medial thigh
It supplies the anterolateral and lateral thigh.
It enters the thigh lateral to the femoral sheath
It lies in the gutter between psoas and iliacus, outside the sheath.
It supplies iliacus within the abdomen
By two or three branches.
Its nerve to vastus medialis travels in the adductor canal and supplies the knee
Hilton's law.
The saphenous nerve crosses the femoral artery from medial to lateral in the adductor canal
The saphenous nerve crosses the artery anteriorly from lateral to medial.
Femoral artery
The artery always lies between the saphenous nerve and the femoral vein.
Saphenous nerve
It leaves the canal between sartorius and gracilis.
Nerve to vastus medialis in its upper part
Last's.
Femoral vein
Last's: the vein spirals from medial to the artery in the femoral triangle to lateral at the adductor hiatus.
It emerges from the medial border of psoas
It crosses the pelvic brim medial to the sacroiliac joint.
Its anterior division supplies adductor longus, brevis and gracilis
And sometimes pectineus. It also supplies the hip joint.
Its posterior division supplies the knee joint
This explains referred knee pain in hip disease.
Its posterior division supplies the ischial part of adductor magnus
The posterior division supplies obturator externus and the adductor (pubic) part of adductor magnus. The ischial (hamstring) part is supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve.

questions.s: Branches of the sacral plexus from posterior divisions include the:
o: Superior gluteal nerve
Nerve to quadratus femoris
Last's: the nerve to quadratus femoris (L4, L5, S1) is from anterior divisions.
Common peroneal part of the sciatic nerve
L4 to S2.
Pudendal nerve
The pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) is from the anterior rami before division.

questions.s: Concerning nerves of the gluteal region:
o: The superior gluteal nerve leaves the pelvis above piriformis
It runs between gluteus medius and minimus and ends in tensor fasciae latae.
The inferior gluteal nerve is L5, S1 and S2
It supplies gluteus maximus.
The nerve to obturator internus hooks around the base of the ischial spine
Lateral to the pudendal vessels. It also supplies superior gemellus.
The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve lies deep to the sciatic nerve
Last's: the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve is superficial to the sciatic, and the nerve to quadratus femoris is deep to it.
It emerges below piriformis, lateral to the inferior gluteal and pudendal bundles
It lies on the ischium over the posterior part of the acetabulum.
Its blood supply includes a branch of the inferior gluteal artery, a remnant of the axial artery
Last's.
The short head of biceps femoris is supplied by its tibial part
The short head of biceps is supplied by the common peroneal part. All other hamstrings and the ischial part of adductor magnus are supplied by the tibial part.
It may divide high, with the peroneal part piercing piriformis
In this case the tibial part runs normally below the muscle.
Divides behind the lateral femoral condyle
It divides in the substance of peroneus longus, around the neck of the fibula.
Gives rise to the sural nerve
The sural nerve arises from the tibial nerve. The common peroneal gives the peroneal communicating nerve, which joins it.
Supplies tibialis posterior
Tibialis posterior is supplied by the tibial nerve.
Gives the lateral cutaneous nerve of the calf
It pierces the roof of the popliteal fossa over the lateral head of gastrocnemius.
The superficial peroneal nerve supplies peroneus longus and brevis
It then perforates the deep fascia halfway down the leg.
The deep peroneal nerve supplies extensor digitorum brevis
And the skin of the first cleft.
The deep peroneal nerve lies medial to the anterior tibial artery throughout the leg
Last's: the deep peroneal nerve runs lateral to the anterior tibial vessels and lies lateral to dorsalis pedis on the foot.
The superficial peroneal nerve supplies most of the dorsum of the foot
Except the first cleft (deep peroneal) and the lateral border (sural).
It is the most superficial of the main structures in the popliteal fossa
The popliteal vein always lies between the artery and the nerve.
It supplies all the muscles arising in the popliteal fossa
Including gastrocnemius, plantaris, soleus and popliteus.
It divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves deep to the flexor retinaculum
Behind the medial malleolus.
The medial calcanean nerve supplies the skin of the lateral border of the foot
It supplies the weight-bearing skin of the heel. The sural nerve supplies the lateral border.
Adductor hallucis
Adductor hallucis is supplied by the deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve.
Flexor hallucis brevis
Medial plantar: FDB, abductor hallucis, FHB and first lumbrical, like the median nerve in the hand.
Flexor digiti minimi brevis
Supplied by the superficial branch of the lateral plantar nerve.
The first lumbrical
The lateral three lumbricals are supplied by the deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve.

questions.s: Structures piercing the roof of the popliteal fossa include the:
o: Tibial nerve
The tibial nerve lies within the fossa, the most superficial of its main contents.
Popliteal artery
The artery is the deepest of the main contents, lying on the floor.
Common peroneal nerve
The common peroneal nerve runs along the lateral boundary medial to biceps. Its branches (lateral cutaneous nerve of the calf and peroneal communicating nerve) pierce the roof.
Small saphenous vein
Last's lists four structures piercing the roof: small saphenous vein, posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, peroneal communicating nerve and lateral cutaneous nerve of the calf.
Arises from the tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa
It lies in the groove between the heads of gastrocnemius.
Pierces the deep fascia halfway down the leg
There it is joined by the peroneal communicating nerve.
Lies medial to the small saphenous vein behind the medial malleolus
It runs lateral to the small saphenous vein behind the lateral malleolus.
Ends on the lateral side of the little toe
It supplies the lateral border of the foot.

questions.s: Regarding the segmental supply of lower limb movements:
o: Hip flexion and adduction are L2 and L3
Hip extension and abduction are L4 and L5.
Knee extension is L3 and L4
Knee flexion is L5 and S1.
Ankle plantarflexion is S1 and S2
Dorsiflexion is L4 and L5.
Inversion of the foot is S1
Inversion (tibialis anterior and posterior) is L4. Eversion is L5 and S1.

questions.s: Concerning nerve supply anomalies noted by Last:
o: Tibialis posterior is supplied by L4 although it is a plantarflexor
It matches its inverting partner, tibialis anterior.
Gluteus maximus and obturator internus are L5, S1 and S2
Other buttock muscles are L4, L5 and S1.
The short head of biceps femoris is supplied by the common peroneal part of the sciatic nerve
It migrated from the extensor compartment.
Pectineus may receive supply from both femoral and obturator nerves
Pectineus, adductor magnus and biceps femoris all have dual supply.

questions.s: Regarding dermatomes of the lower limb:
o: L1 supplies the inguinal region and anterior scrotum
Last's.
L5 supplies the dorsum of the foot and great toe
Also the lateral leg.
S1 supplies the lateral border of the foot and sole
And the lateral malleolus.
S3 supplies the posterior thigh
S2 supplies the posterior thigh and leg. S3 supplies the sitting area of the buttock and posterior scrotum.
The main blood supply to the femoral head in adults is from retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery
The artery of the ligamentum teres is minor in adults.
The iliofemoral ligament resists extension
It is the strongest ligament in the body.
It is supplied by the femoral, obturator and sciatic nerves
Including the nerve to quadratus femoris.
The neck of the femur ossifies from a separate epiphysis
Last's: the neck is the upper end of the shaft and ossifies as part of it.

questions.s: The knee joint receives nerve supply from the:
o: Femoral nerve via the nerve to vastus medialis
Last's (Hilton's law).
Genicular branches of the tibial and common peroneal nerves
From the sciatic nerve.
Posterior division of the obturator nerve
Running with the femoral artery through the adductor hiatus.
Saphenous nerve via its infrapatellar branch
It supplies the front of the knee and patellar plexus.

questions.s: Regarding ossification in the lower limb:
o: The centre for the lower end of the femur appears at birth and is medicolegal evidence of maturity
Last's.
The fibula is exceptional in that its upper (growing) end ossifies later than its lower end
Head at 4 years, lower end at 1 year.
The cuboid ossifies at about 9 months of fetal life
Its presence is also evidence of maturity.
Most growth in length of the lower limb occurs at the hip
Growth proceeds more rapidly at the knee than at the hip or ankle.

questions.s: Concerning veins of the lower limb:
o: The great saphenous vein marks the preaxial border of the limb
The small saphenous marks the postaxial border.
The great saphenous vein passes in front of the medial malleolus with the saphenous nerve
A site for venous cutdown.
The femoral vein lies lateral to the femoral artery at the adductor hiatus
Last's: it spirals from medial (in the triangle) to lateral (at the hiatus).
The small saphenous vein drains into the femoral vein
It pierces the roof of the popliteal fossa to drain into the popliteal vein.
